stories.title: One small business. $2M in exports to the U.S. And now, $1M in tariff costs
stories.summary: Ed’s Concrete in Stratford is a small, local example of how tariffs and international trade disputes hit home.
stories.author: Norman De Bono
stories.content:
The tariff war between Canada and the U.S. has created a million-dollar problem for one concrete business in Stratford.

Exclusive articles from Ryan Pyette, Dale Carruthers, Jane Sims, Norman De Bono and others. Plus, the Noon News Roundup newsletter on weekdays and the LFP Weekender newsletter on weekends.

The U.S. administration recently hit a long list of unique Canadian business sectors with the 50 per cent import tax. Ed’s Concrete in Stratford is among the affected businesses – a small, local example of how tariffs and international trade disputes hit home.

The business, which makes concrete products, will have to now pay about $1 million annually on its $2 million in export sales to the U.S., general manager Byron Veldjesgraaf said.

That’s a big hit for a small business.

“This is not ideal, it’s not sustainable,” Veldjesgraaf said.

After tariff and trade talks between Canada and the U.S. broke down last week, the U.S. levied 50 per cent tariffs on $28 billion worth of goods shipped from Canada into America. It is also considering increasing tariffs on vehicles and auto parts to 50 per cent in January.

Canada announced Tuesday it will hit the U.S. with a series of counter-tariffs on $27.6 billion worth of goods, starting in September.

Veldjesgraaf is now looking at import codes that apply to products sold into the U.S. to see if he can ship his concrete products south of the border under different codes to avoid tariffs.

“We’re reassuring customers we’ll eat tariffs for now” until the business can use different import codes, he said. “Each product can fall under different codes that aren’t tariffed.”

Exports to the U.S. make up about 10 per cent of his business and if it can’t get tariff relief, they May have to cut costs including staffing reductions. “That could happen, absolutely, if there’s a reduction in our exports. This is bad for the Canadian economy.”

Ed’s makes concrete products, including “architectural” pieces such as benches and large planters. It has supplied Ford Motor Co. headquarters in Dearborn, Michigan.

Trump’s 50% auto tariff threat rattles Southwestern Ontario manufacturers

Pierre Poilievre on jacked-up tariffs: 'We have what the Americans need'

Jason Bates is director of the London Region Manufacturing Council. He believes the 50 per cent tariffs will have a limited impact in Southwestern Ontario. He’s hearing little about it driving up costs but he’s concerned about the toll on business investment and confidence because tariffs create uncertainty.

“It’s an odd list” of businesses being hit by President Donald Trump’s new tariffs, he said. “It’s mostly small businesses that will feel it. But it adds to the confusion, the frustration and May slow investment as some businesses are taking a wait-and-see attitude” about future growth and investment.

“It’s frustrating.”

While some wood products are hit with the additional export fees, Element5, the fast-growing business in St. Thomas that uses wood in construction and has expanded into the U.S., has dodged the tariff bullet, said its president, Chris Latour.

“We’re not impacted but we’re still concerned,” Latour said. “People in small businesses are adding up costs now and not going ahead with projects they planned. This uncertainty is a challenge.

“Construction companies have to price plywood, toilets and sinks and they don’t know what their costs are. Widespread tariffs of any sort will impact decision-making in every industry.”

stories.title: Local animal rescue cleared to resume adoptions after four-month halt
stories.summary: The rescue is reopening adoptions while an animal-welfare investigation and appeal over a nearly $200,000 bill continue.
stories.author: Allison Young
stories.content:
The rescue is reopening adoptions while an animal-welfare investigation and appeal over a nearly $200,000 bill continue.

After a nearly four-month halt in finding homes for its animals, a St. Thomas animal rescue has been cleared to resume adoptions.

Exclusive articles from Ryan Pyette, Dale Carruthers, Jane Sims, Norman De Bono and others. Plus, the Noon News Roundup newsletter on weekdays and the LFP Weekender newsletter on weekends.

Saving Animals’ Lives Together (Salt) Rescue Organization received approval to reopen its daily adoption hours following a visit from Provincial Animal Welfare Services on Friday. The rescue was initially directed to halt adoptions after an April 30 inspection led to an ongoing animal-welfare investigation.

The inspection resulted in about 60 cats being taken into provincial care, with 17 later euthanized. Salt was also issued a nearly $200,000 bill for veterinary and boarding costs associated with the animals in provincial care.

The Free Press contacted the Ministry of the Solicitor General for comment but did not receive a response.

“It’s been very difficult every day, even now it is. I just want these animals to find their homes,” Salt owner Bonnie Smith said.

The return of adoptions comes as Salt continues to face financial pressure. Smith said the rescue is trying to raise money through a GoFundMe campaign to help pay the $198,165.28 statement of account while also covering ongoing veterinary bills and other operating costs.

Tuesday was the deadline to settle the statement of account, but Smith said payment has been paused while Salt goes through the appeal process.

Smith said donations have declined amid criticism of herself and the rescue. Since it began Aug. 16, the GoFundMe campaign has raised $2,335, less than two per cent of its goal.

“We just don’t have the money because many people aren’t donating. I think it’s because of all the negativity out there, which is unfortunate because the cats are the ones that are going to suffer,” Smith said.

After halting adoptions for months, the rescue will not be taking in new animals. Smith said she wants the animals already at Salt to find homes rather than spend more time in cages.

17 cats euthanized without consent of local animal rescue

She also said the number of animals at the rescue was one factor that contributed to it becoming overwhelmed.

“This has been a nightmare and we do not want to have this reoccurring, so we are going to be not taking a lot of animals right now, maybe even in the future. We can’t get into this situation ever again,” Smith said.

stories.title: Kirsten Krose promises traffic plan, city hall dashboard in mayoral platform
stories.summary: The mayoral candidate says her plan is built around the issues she hears about most from Londoners.
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
The mayoral candidate says her plan is built around the issues she hears about most from Londoners.

The first to register and the first to release a platform, mayoral candidate Kirsten Krose has unveiled her campaign promises, including a plan for her first 100 days in office.

Exclusive articles from Ryan Pyette, Dale Carruthers, Jane Sims, Norman De Bono and others. Plus, the Noon News Roundup newsletter on weekdays and the LFP Weekender newsletter on weekends.

Released early this week, Krose’s platform focuses on four main pillars: public safety, better city services, better traffic management and restrained taxpayer spending – all linked by a fifth campaign element: housing.

“After talking extensively at the door to different organizations, to different groups, different people, businesses, everything, there were a lot of recurring themes. Traffic was a really big one. Homelessness, feeling safe downtown, safe in other areas, safe on the roads, public transit,” she told The Free Press Tuesday.

“These all kind of just kept coming up, and if the taxpayers . . . are the ones complaining about it, that’s really where we need to be focusing – because clearly they’re not satisfied.”

On public safety, Krose promises elements of both policing and city-building measures, including preventing homelessness through rent and eviction supports and faster navigation of the housing system. On policing, she calls for a greater focus on crime while improving co-ordinated responses to mental health, addictions and homelessness-related calls.

On transportation, one of her first 100-day pledges is to create a “traffic bottleneck program” to evaluate London’s most congested intersections and corridors, as well as school zones for risk.

Boosting transit reliability and frequency is another element, along with evaluating the results of bus rapid transit once it fully launches.

On spending and city services, the platform includes a housing report card, modernizing development approvals, a review of all city departments and, most crucially to Krose, a public city hall performance dashboard.

paragraphs: London, Ont. (Aug. 24, 2026) – A London man is facing multiple charges after police were called to a break and enter at a residence in the south end of the city over the weekend.

On Saturday, August 22, 2026, at about 6:10 a.m., an elderly woman was woken by a loud noise and found a man entering the residence in the area of Wellington Road and Base Line Road East. The victim was assaulted and stabbed before she was able to call 911.

Multiple officers responded. As officers attended the residence the accused began throwing broken glass at police. One officer sustained minor injuries. Officers entered the residence, and arrested the suspect.
The victim was transported to hospital by paramedic services with serious but non-life-threatening injuries. The suspect was transported to hospital by paramedic services with minor injuries.
The suspect and victim were not known to each other.
As a result of the investigation, Nelson Enrique Cornejo, 40, of London, has been charged with the following offences:
Aggravated assault;
Break and enter with intent;
Assault a peace officer with a weapon; and
Obstruct peace officer.
The accused remains in custody and is expected to re-appear in London court August 27, 2026, in relation to the charges.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips (8477). Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: St. Thomas considers tougher approach to vacant downtown storefronts
stories.summary: The city is weighing monthly fire inspections and other measures to encourage landlords to fill vacant properties.
stories.author: Brian Williams
stories.content:
The city is weighing monthly fire inspections and other measures to encourage landlords to fill vacant properties.

St. Thomas is exploring ways to entice landlords of empty downtown storefronts and buildings to fill vacancies in the growing community, Mayor Joe Preston says.

Exclusive articles from Ryan Pyette, Dale Carruthers, Jane Sims, Norman De Bono and others. Plus, the Noon News Roundup newsletter on weekdays and the LFP Weekender newsletter on weekends.

Although there May be the “fewest (number) of vacant stores” downtown since Preston moved to St. Thomas roughly 35 years ago, he said there are still “some investors who believe that just the asset growth in their property is enough,” and the city is looking at ways to address those vacancies.

“We’ve been looking at a number of different ways and looking at some other communities that have been trying to address vacant storefronts or vacant buildings in their own right,” Preston said, pointing to Oakville, which has a bylaw requiring inspections of vacant buildings.

One option St. Thomas is considering is more frequent fire inspections.

“We’re working on a plan that makes our fire inspection team inspect the buildings once a month and at a little cost to the landlord, which May inspire them to actually make them not vacant buildings and not make them vacant storefronts,” he said.

Preston pointed to a “couple of major fires” in recent years, including a July 2025 arson fire downtown that destroyed a 144-year-old building and caused $1 million in damage. He said the close proximity of buildings in the core can create dangerous conditions during a fire.

There have been discussions among city council and the fire department about potentially implementing a bylaw to enforce fire inspections, Preston said.

“(The) fire inspection team and the chief have been talking about how to best write the bylaw because it really would take a certain bylaw (to enforce),” he said.

Preston also said any tax breaks once available for vacant storefronts were removed during his tenure as mayor, meaning landlords pay the same tax bill whether a building is occupied or not.

St. Thomas hits key milestone in push to end homelessness

New St. Thomas sculpture puts colourful spin on railway roots

“We want to make sure, first of all, from a safety point of view, and from an incentive of a landlord who’s sitting with an empty storefront to do something else with it,” Preston said.

“There is way more activity right now among landlords to really renovate and move forward anyway, but if we can offer some incentive for them not to leave the storefronts empty, then we’ll move as fast as we can on it.”

Downtown storefronts have been gradually filling over the past several years, Preston said, crediting in part the city’s introduction of special constables to the core.

“(It makes) downtown safe for people to be there and welcoming, and that’s really made quite a difference,” he said. “Almost once a week there’s another new business opening up somewhere.”

Commercial growth is also visible elsewhere.

Preston said downtown “becomes the next place to be” after businesses have flocked to the “absolutely full and growing” SmartCentres outdoor shopping centre and the Elgin Centre mall.

The city’s commercial growth comes amid an industrial boom, with Volkswagen subsidiary PowerCo’s $7-billion EV battery plant expected to open in 2027 and eventually employ 3,000 people, along with nearby Vianode’s planned factory.

“I would say, in my whole 35 years in St. Thomas, this is as vibrant a downtown as we’ve had to this point,” Preston said.

“There’s no stopping US now. There’s still vacancy. There’s still people who need a place to do commercial activity in our community.”

stories.title: Satan’s Choice president rips anti-patch law targeting Hells Angels
stories.summary: The debate follows recent sightings of patch-wearing Hells Angels members at London restaurants.
stories.author: Dale Carruthers
stories.content:
The debate follows recent sightings of patch-wearing Hells Angels members at London restaurants.

The head of Canada’s fastest-growing outlaw motorcycle club is blasting a recent decision to ban public displays promoting the Hells Angels logo in Quebec.

Exclusive articles from Ryan Pyette, Dale Carruthers, Jane Sims, Norman De Bono and others. Plus, the Noon News Roundup newsletter on weekdays and the LFP Weekender newsletter on weekends.

The Quebec crackdown follows a series of sightings of Hells Angels members wearing their patches at London restaurants, a move one organized crime expert says is meant to intimidate rival bikers in Southwestern Ontario.

In April, Quebec passed Bill 13, known as the anti-patch law, to reinforce public safety by barring the public display of names and images associated with an “entity with a criminal purpose.” The law allows Public Security Minister Ian Lafrenière to declare certain organizations criminal groups and bars those groups from displaying symbols to promote themselves.

Lafrenière signed a decree last week saying the Hells Angels will be the first criminal group targeted by the law.

“When three Hells Angels walk into a restaurant wearing their jackets, it’s not usually just to go eat . . . it’s to intimidate people and often to collect money,” said Maxime Tardif, a spokesperson for Lafrenière’s office.

The law, which takes effect Sept. 2, applies to the Hells Angels name, the club’s Death Head logo and other symbols and acronyms such as 81, representing H and A in the alphabet, and Affa, or Angels Forever, Forever Angels.

Police can demand individuals wearing clothing promoting the Hells Angels remove it or risk being fined or having the items seized.

News that the world’s largest outlaw motorcycle club will be the first targeted by the anti-patch law drew criticism from many in the one-per-cent biker community, including Satan’s Choice national president Harley Guindon.

“It’s a sad thing that’s happening to our country. Our freedoms being stripped . . . this is getting ridiculous,” Guindon wrote on social media. “Just spend more taxpayers money for something that won’t stop anything.”

Patch-wearing Hells Angels turn up at London restaurants as biker rivalry grows

New figures shed light on police efforts to thwart Ontario outlaw bikers

Guindon, former vice-president of the Brooklin, Ont., chapter of the Hells Angels, revived the club his father helped launch decades ago. Since relaunching Satan’s Choice last year, the club has opened 50 chapters across Canada, including three in Southwestern Ontario.

Guindon said he hopes his former club mounts a legal challenge against the anti-patch law “for everyone.”

Lawyers representing the Hells Angels have previously vowed to challenge the law, according to a report from The Globe and Mail.

The Hells Angels have a long and bloody history in Quebec. The club, founded in Fontana, Calif., in 1948, opened its first Canadian chapter in Montreal in 1977. Over the decades, the Hells Angels have fought turf battles with rival motorcycle clubs, street gangs and mafia groups in Quebec.

The debate over whether outlaw bikers should be able to wear their patches in public was recently reignited in London after a group of Hells Angels were spotted at a south-end steakhouse and another member on the patio of an Old South restaurant.

Ontario doesn’t have any laws prohibiting public displays promoting outlaw biker clubs, but police in several cities have launched programs barring individuals from wearing biker- and gang-affiliated clothing inside businesses.

Police in participating cities provide signs with the words “No Gang Colours, No Gang Clothing” to local businesses and say the policy is enforced through the Trespass to Property Act. Businesses are instructed to call police to remove patrons violating the rule.

With files from The Montreal Gazette

stories.title: London Knights training camp: Blue line a clear strength as OHL season nears
stories.summary: London Knights, Maksim Sokolovskii, Henry Brzustewicz, Easton Cowan, OHL, junior hockey, CHL
stories.author: Ryan Pyette
stories.content:
Maksim Sokolovskii got a lot of social media mileage out of flipping a 1,000-pound tire during his summer workouts.

Exclusive articles from Ryan Pyette, Dale Carruthers, Jane Sims, Norman De Bono and others. Plus, the Noon News Roundup newsletter on weekdays and the LFP Weekender newsletter on weekends.

But being nearly 6-foot-8 and 240 pounds won’t shield the big defenceman from the expected playful jabs about it in the early days at London Knights training camp.

“I told him the real workers work in silence,” Henry Brzustewicz, the L.A. Kings first-rounder, joked. “They don’t need to film themselves and stuff like that.”

Was that impressive TikTok video a sign that the gregarious Russian has grown too big for his britches in his second year with the famous OHL franchise?

“Maybe,” Brzustewicz said.

Sokolovskii thought carefully, then mustered up his most threatening glance.

“I’ll say (to him), ‘See you on the ice,’” the Flyers first-rounder warned before breaking into laughter.

The obvious strength of the Knights this season is the blue line. The biggest questions right now are how much has Sokolovskii improved and will Brzustewicz ever play another regular-season game in London?

“So busy summer,” the 18-year-old man mountain said. “Back-to-back Russia to North America around four times. I was in Philly (development) camp. Really enjoyed it. I was with (Denver Barkey and Oliver Bonk) and we had a very good time together.”

His confidence in speaking English and playing at an elevated level has grown immensely since he arrived in London.

“So much better,” he said. “Of course, it helped me so much (being with the Knights) last year. It’s like a mini-NHL team here.”

To a man, the returning players see last year’s first-round playoff loss to Sault Ste. Marie as an unfortunate blip.

“Memorial Cup, that’s the goal,” Sokolovskii said. “We have a really good team and will work to win games.”

In small-town Watford, a homegrown player returns with his London Knights

‘London’s always first’: Knights sign first-round pick Kane Barch

It’s hard to argue with a guy who can flip a 1,000-pound tire.

SO Long?: The Knights are understandably bracing themselves for losing Brzustewicz to the pro ranks this fall.

A new and controversial rule will allow NHL first-rounders to stay in the American Hockey League even if they have major junior eligibility remaining. The 19-year-old Michigander is already one of Los Angeles’s prize prospects and will use this time with the Knights as a springboard to a successful Kings training camp.

“Being able to play in scrimmages here and get into game shape with some preseason should be good for getting my game going,” he said. “(Being in London) helps you a lot. It’s the most pro guys there are and (the Hunters) know what they’re doing.

“We went to a good situation here and you want to show you’re ready for the next step. When I go (to L.A.), I just want to play my game, show what I’ve got, play with confidence and do what I can to give myself the best chance for that opportunity.”

For now, he plans to be an example.

“I hope I can,” he said. “You want the Knights to do well every year even if you’re not playing there. You just want to be a good role model and leader to the younger guys. There are some high-calibre leadership guys here (already).”

Around THE Rink: Knights grad Easton Cowan was at Canada Life Place Monday filming a commercial. He is expected to go on the ice here ahead of Maple Leafs training camp, as will back-to-back Memorial Cup champions Sam O’Reilly (Lightning) and Jared Woolley (Kings) after their successful run with Kitchener. “It’s awesome,” London associate GM Rob Simpson said. “It gives our new players and younger guys a real understanding of, this is how you have to compete, this is how you practice and these are the details you need in your game if you’re going to be a first-round NHL pick or legitimate prospect beyond our league. We love when those guys come out because it’s a good learning experience for everybody else.” . . . Will Swedish import forward Marcus Nordmark play in London this season? That question won’t be answered until after the Anaheim first-rounder attends Ducks training camp. The 18-year-old is currently skating with the Swedish national team until the end of the week . . . As always, there are deep hockey roots at Knights camp. London’s 2026 first-rounder Ryan Beaulieu, of course, is the son of 2005 Memorial Cup champ Josh Beaulieu, Ewan Sim is the 16-year-old brother of 2025 Memorial Cup champ and 2026 Calder Cup champ Landon Sim, Jaxon Welychka’s cousin Brett played for the Knights from 2010-15 and Anthony Thomas-Maroon’s dad Pat was here in 2007-08 before a long NHL career. Even more recently, Dylan Wilmott is the younger brother of Ben Wilmott, who was a top scorer for London last season before being dealt to the Barrie Colts and drafted by Vegas in the third round. . . . It doesn’t stop there. Recently signed forward Kane Barch’s father Krys is a former Knight who will do some development work with London after coaching the Niagara IceDogs last year. Ryker Kesler is the son of former NHLer Ryan Kesler and Bradley Marchant’s dad Todd was a long-time Edmonton Oiler and Anaheim Duck. . . . Import forward Luca Santala, who represented Finland at the Hlinka Gretzky Cup, grew up with father Tommi playing pro hockey in Europe and a couple of NHL stints with Atlanta and Vancouver. Santala was at his playmaking best in some of the early Knights scrimmages . . . Up-and-coming defenceman Cooper McAslan, a London Nationals star last year, will miss some early camp time with a lower-body injury. He won gold with Canada at the Hlinka Gretzky Cup with an 8-1 victory over the United States in the final . . . stories.title: Ontario Premier Doug Ford admits ‘it got a little heated’ with President Donald Trump
stories.summary: 'Things got a little heated, it got a little personal yesterday,' Premier Doug Ford told CNN on Tuesday morning, agreeing with Wolf Blitzer it is time to lower the temperature.
stories.author: Isaac Callan, Colin D'Mello
stories.content:
If you get Global News from Instagram or Facebook - that will be changing. Find out how you can still connect with US .

After calling President Donald Trump a “loser” and the “king of bankruptcies” who could “kiss my ass,” Ontario Premier Doug Ford is embarking on a tour of United States news networks, striking a more conciliatory tone.

“Things got a little heated, it got a little personal yesterday,” Premier Doug Ford told CNN on Tuesday morning, agreeing with Wolf Blitzer that it was time to lower the temperature.

“I want to make a deal. A good deal for the American people, a good deal for the Canadians. We’re the two greatest countries in the world, we’re each other’s number one customer and it’s time to get back to the table.”

The more measured tone came the day after Trump described Ford as “the less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother of the late, great, Rob Ford” in a post on Truth Social.

During a 45-minute news conference, the Ontario premier repeatedly hit back.

“I don’t respond to a dictator like President Trump, a bully like President Trump,” Ford told reporters. “I’m not going to take any advice off a guy that’s the king of bankruptcies.”

Later, he concluded: “Let’s be clear, I don’t like the guy — simple.”

Then, ON Tuesday morning, Trump posted online again, this time musing about renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America as relations between the president and Canada’s most populous province deteriorated.

The change would be similar to the Republican president’s executive order last year to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America.

The Great Lakes — Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie and Superior — are a chain of five freshwater lakes that hold roughly one-fifth of the world’s surface fresh water. Lake Ontario, which the province is named after, shares a border with the U.S. states of New York and Pennsylvania.

Michigan is the only Great Lake that doesn’t border Canada.

Ford, however, didn’t bite back in his interview with CNN.

“I think it’s a lot of rhetoric,” he told Blitzer. “When President Trump wants to attack our sovereignty and attack our businesses and people in Ontario, I can’t roll over. My job is to protect Ontario and Canada.”

The premier was at Queen’s Park on Tuesday to record various United States news segments, but didn’t stop to speak to Ontario reporters.

As the premier walked from one room to another at the Ontario legislature, he batted away the idea that his rhetoric had gone too far on Monday.

“No, not at all,” he said. “Not at all.”

Ford is also scheduled to appear on ABC News, CBS and Bloomberg Washington throughout the day.

The United States and Canada are locked in a trade dispute after Prime Minister Mark Carney suspended trade talks last Friday, accusing the U.S. of trying to introduce last-minute demands that would limit Canada’s ability to make trade deals with other countries and protect its culture and sovereignty.

The U.S. introduced a new round of 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian exports on Saturday, targeting goods worth $28 billion. Canada announced retaliatory measures Tuesday that will go into effect Sept. 8.

— with files from Global News’ Aaron D’Andrea

stories.title: Extortion trial dates set for former London city councillor
stories.summary: Miriam Hamou, a former Ward 6 politician, was charged in November with extortion and harassing communications.
stories.author: Jane Sims
stories.content:
A former London city councillor is heading to trial next year on extortion and harassment charges.

Exclusive articles from Ryan Pyette, Dale Carruthers, Jane Sims, Norman De Bono and others. Plus, the Noon News Roundup newsletter on weekdays and the LFP Weekender newsletter on weekends.

Miriam Hamou, 51, was charged in November with extortion and harassing communications after an investigation headed up by the St. Thomas police.

A court-ordered publication ban protects the identity of the complainant.

Hamou’s defence lawyer, Laura Ellis, made a quick video court appearance before justice of the peace Chantal Bertrand in a London courtroom Tuesday where she confirmed that Hamou is scheduled to have a two-day Ontario Court of Justice trial on Feb. 26 and March 2.

Hamou was not in court for the brief appearance and was not required to attend.

Hamou represented Ward 6 for about a year after former city councillor Phil Squire stepped away from city hall politics. She was appointed in November 2021, but narrowly lost her seat the following year in the civic election to Coun. Sam Trosow.

Following the charges, Hamou resigned from the London Health Sciences Centre’s community advisory committee, saying publicly that “I don’t want to bring any negativity or anything toward LHSC while I am under investigation.”

Hamou served on several boards and committees before her appointment to council.

The St. Thomas police were called in to investigate the London-based complaint to ensure no conflict of interest, as required by the Community Safety and Policing Act.

No other details about the investigation were released by the police at the time of the charges.

Hamou’s case was brought before the Ontario Court several times over the past months for case management before the trial dates were set on Tuesday.

stories.title: 2 arrested after homemade electric weapon, drugs seized in theft investigation
stories.summary: On Aug. 21, officers executed a search warrant at a property where they seized approximately 50 grams of suspected methamphetamine, two grams of suspected fentanyl and other items.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Two Ontario men have been charged after an investigation into stolen property led to the seizure of more than 50 grams of suspected methamphetamine, fentanyl and a homemade electric weapon.

OPP began an investigation earlier this month after receiving reports of stolen property in the South Frontenac area.

On Aug. 21, officers executed a search warrant at a property where they seized approximately 50 grams of suspected methamphetamine, two grams of suspected fentanyl, assorted pills, a camper trailer, an ATV, a dirt bike, assorted hand tools, approximately $1,000 and digital scales.

A homemade conducted energy weapon, a device that uses electrical current to stun a person, was also found.

As a result of the investigation, a 38-year-old man has been charged with two counts of possession of property obtained by crime over $5,000, one count of possession of property obtained by crime under $5,000, three counts of drug possession for the purpose of trafficking and possession of ammunition and a weapon for a dangerous purpose.

A 57-year-old man was also arrested and charged with failure to comply with a release order.

stories.title: Abandoned puppies now in foster homes after found in box in Brantford
stories.summary: The puppies were sent to Sato Saved End of the Line Dog Rescue and Rehabilitation as Hillside Kennels Animal Control noted they need special attention and require bottle feeding.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
An animal control in an Ontario city and a dog rescue say several puppies abandoned have found loving fosters to help in their care, but are reminding the public there’s “no excuse for dumping puppies.”

Hillside Kennels Animal Control, which works with the City of Brantford, posted on Monday that it had picked up 11 puppies that appeared to be one to two days old from a box found in the city earlier that morning.

The puppies, which appear to be bully breed-type dogs, were found with no mother in sight.

“There is no excuse for dumping puppies,” the animal control wrote on Facebook. “We worry about the mom who May be worried where they have gone or that she May have passed away.”

It said it had turned over the puppies to Sato Saved End of the Line Dog Rescue and Rehabilitation, as they need special attention and require bottle feeding.

The dog rescue said in its own Facebook post that one of the puppies has a cleft palate and will need to be tube fed.

Sato Saved issued a plea for help from experienced fosters who have bottle-fed before and are within 30 minutes of Brantford, offering to supply anything the fosters would need.

“Puppies will need to be fed every three hours for the next four weeks,” the post reads. “If you can’t wake up overnight don’t apply because it’s very important they are kept on a schedule.”

Fosters were later secured, the dog rescue said in an update to its post, adding that two puppies had also been transferred to Travelling Tails K9 Rescue.

Animal control is asking if anyone knows who dumped the puppies to please contact animal welfare at 1-833-926-4625.

stories.title: Ontario students brace for ‘vast amount’ of debt amid Osap changes, tuition increases
stories.summary: As of Aug. 1, the proportion of non-repayable grants a student can receive through Osap has been reduced from 85 per cent to a maximum of 25 per cent, with the rest given in loans.
stories.author: Monique Kasonga
stories.content:
As Aidan Jeffers begins his graduate studies at the University of Toronto, he says he will have to work more hours and possibly rely on food banks due to drastic changes to student financial aid in Ontario – and the resulting debt he expects to rack up.

Jeffers said he’s been working two jobs over the summer as large student loans weigh on his mind. He also plans to work 25 or 30 hours a week during the school year.

“I might have to go to the food bank a couple of times,” said Jeffers, an incoming master’s student in library and information science. “I’ll be working during my master’s instead of completely locking in.”

Earlier this year, Premier Doug Ford’s government announced it would sharply cut student assistance grants, citing “unsustainable” costs. As of Aug. 1, the proportion of non-repayable grants a student can receive through the Ontario Student Assistance Program has been reduced from 85 per cent to a maximum of 25 per cent, with the rest given in loans.

The province also lifted a seven-year tuition fee freeze, allowing colleges and universities to raise tuition by up to two per cent per year for the next three years.

Post-secondary students across the province are now bracing for the impact of those changes as a new school year approaches. Many have said that significantly scaled-back Osap grants will saddle them with high debt loads amid economic uncertainty.

Jeffers said he relied on Osap throughout his undergraduate studies and will continue to do so in graduate school.

“The biggest change is the amount of actual loans I’ll be getting, as opposed to the grants,” Jeffers said. “My tuition costs have also gone up.”

With 85 per cent of his Osap funding now being loans, Jeffers said he’s “incurring a vast amount more debt” than he did in his undergraduate years. He said he’ll be receiving around $19,500 this year, of which $12,000 will go toward tuition.

The Osap changes were announced after Jeffers had already decided to pursue his master’s, but he still had enough time to calculate his costs and come up with a plan before starting school.

“I’m even still one of the lucky ones, because I can adjust and say, ‘OK, this is what I thought the expenditure was going to be, but now I know it’s going to be this much, and this is how much debt I’m going to incur,'” he said.

“It’s still very stressful. But for people who are in the middle of their master’s or their undergrad, it’s definitely a big change.”

Jeffers said some of his peers have decided not to pursue graduate studies due to the amount of debt they would have to take on.

Rory Norris, president of the Ontario Undergraduate Student Alliance and a recent University of Waterloo graduate, said it’s hard to measure how the changes will affect students this year, since many are only now discovering what their Osap funding will look like.

Norris said many students rely on the online Osap calculator to plan their finances in advance, but it was only recently updated to reflect the funding changes.

He said surveys conducted by the student alliance over the years have shown how much Ontario students’ education depends on Osap.

“When it comes to what students rely on to support themselves in post-secondary, (Osap) is the highest ranked out of anything, even ahead of part-time jobs and family,” he said. “Even before the changes took place, over 80 per cent of students said Osap was their highest form of financial aid.”

Ishan Bijukuchhay, a computer engineering student at Queen’s University, said his Osap funding was 60 per cent grants and 40 per cent loans in his first year of study.

“Now it’s more like 85 per cent loans and 15 per cent grants,” he said. “I wasn’t anticipating this much of a switch.”

Bijukuchhay said his overall Osap funding has also dropped by about $3,000.

He has worked as a lifeguard to help cover his expenses, and he recently learned that he automatically qualified for Queen’s work-study program, which will help offset the Osap grant cuts. He has also received bursaries from the university but said a tuition fee increase means he will continue to be reliant on both Osap and the school’s financial services.

Beyond tuition, “there’s rent, there’s fees, there’s supplies,” Bijukuchhay said.

“I will continue to seek out assistance to afford fees for the traditional university experience for events in upcoming years, such as my engineering discipline banquet and the science formal, among other events,” he said.

The Ontario government says Osap grant cuts were necessary.

“For this fiscal year 2025-26, Osap costs ballooned even further to $2.7 billion. If our government did not make these changes, Osap would have cost $4.1 billion by 2028-29,” Bianca Giacoboni, a spokesperson for Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn, wrote in a statement.

Data previously obtained by The Canadian Press through a freedom-of-information request shows that between the 2023-24 and 2024-25 academic years, the province spent $465 million more on Osap grants, and 95 per cent of that went to private career college students. Opposition critics have said that shows the government did not have to penalize students at universities and publicly funded colleges with across-the-board grant cuts.

Giacoboni said the government will continue to support qualified low-income students through the Ontario Learn and Stay Grant and Student Access Guarantee programs.

The tuition fee increases will result in an “additional cost of $0.18 per day for college students and $0.47 a day for university students” on average, her statement said.

Norris, the head of the Ontario Undergraduate Student Alliance, said the group representing about 160,000 students across the province believes changes are needed to the Osap loan repayment model itself. Removing interest on provincial student loans is even more important now that their amounts will be higher, he said.

In 2023, the federal government eliminated interest on the federal portion of student loans. Ontario and Saskatchewan remain the only two provinces where interest accrues on the provincial portions of student loans.

Norris also said the Osap repayment grace period should be extended past the current six months. That would give students more flexibility, he said, pointing to data that suggests it’s taking university graduates longer to find work.

A November 2025 report by the student alliance group found that unemployment rates for Ontario youth with a bachelor’s degree was nearly 12 per cent, versus the national rate of nine per cent.

Statistics Canada data shows that 25 per cent of college students and 50 per cent of university undergraduate students in Ontario had more than $25,000 in debt at graduation in 2020, comparable to national figures from that year.

Accumulating even more debt through Osap May not be an option for many, advocates say.

“You’re delaying all these other life milestones, like buying a house, starting a family, just because you’re putting so much of this money that you’d traditionally be able to do those sorts of things with into these repayments that you’re having to make,” Norris said.

Bijukuchhay, the Queen’s University student, said he was 17 years old at the time of the last provincial election and he is now more interested in politics after seeing how government policy affects students. His peers are also more aware of those issues, he said.

“They definitely have to feel more aware of their finances, and be more aware of the government and its policies, and how those policies affect them day to day — and in the future, too,” he said.

stories.title: Trump considering renaming Lake Ontario as relations with province sour
stories.summary: President Donald Trump says the United States is giving 'serious consideration' to renaming one of the Great Lakes as relations with Canada's most populated province sour.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:

President Donald Trump says the United States is giving “serious consideration” to renaming one of the Great Lakes as relations with Canada’s most populated province sour.

Trump posted on Truth Social Tuesday morning that he’s thinking of changing the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America.”

“The United States is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don’t expect to be doing much business with Ontario any longer,” he wrote.

He later posted a graphic illustrating a name change.

The change would be similar to the Republican president’s executive order last year to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America.

The Great Lakes — Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie and Superior — are a chain of five freshwater lakes that hold roughly one-fifth of the world’s surface fresh water. Lake Ontario, which the province is named after, shares a border with the U.S. state of New York.

Michigan is the only Great Lake that doesn’t border Canada.

The United States and Canada are locked in a trade dispute after Prime Minister Mark Carney suspended trade talks last Friday, accusing the U.S. of trying to introduce last-minute demands that would limit Canada’s ability to make trade deals with other countries and protect its culture and sovereignty.

The U.S. introduced a new round of 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian exports on Saturday, targeting goods worth $28 billion. Canada announced retaliatory measures Tuesday that will go into effect Sept. 8.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is home to the country’s auto industry, said Monday that he backs Carney. He also took aim at Trump after the president posted about him on social media.

“I don’t respond to a dictator like President Trump, a bully like President Trump. I’m not going to take any advice off a guy that’s the king of bankruptcies,” Ford said during a news conference , which also heard him say Trump could “kiss my ass.”

“Let’s be clear, I don’t like the guy — simple.”

Ford told Cnn’s Wolf Blitzer Tuesday morning “things got a little personal” with Trump on Monday.

He said Trump’s Lake Ontario post was “a lot of rhetoric,” and it’s time to tone it down.

“I want to make a good deal for the American people, a good deal for the Canadians,” he said.

“We’re the two greatest countries in the world. We’re each other’s No. 1 customer and it’s time to get back to the table and let’s negotiate a fair deal because it’s hurting the U.S., it’s hurting Canada and we just want to make sure that we have a fair deal.”

Carney said Monday that Canada will go back to the negotiating table on a trade deal once the United States changes its attitude and stops treating Canada as a subsidiary.

content_blocks.text: President Donald Trump says the United States is giving “serious consideration” to renaming one of the Great Lakes as relations with Canada’s most populated province sour.
Trump posted on Truth Social Tuesday morning that he’s thinking of changing the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America.”
“The United States is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don’t expect to be doing much business with Ontario any longer,” he wrote.
He later posted a graphic illustrating a name change.
The change would be similar to the Republican president’s executive order last year to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America.

The Great Lakes — Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie and Superior — are a chain of five freshwater lakes that hold roughly one-fifth of the world’s surface fresh water. Lake Ontario, which the province is named after, shares a border with the U.S. state of New York.
Get daily National news
Michigan is the only Great Lake that doesn’t border Canada.

The United States and Canada are locked in a trade dispute after Prime Minister Mark Carney suspended trade talks last Friday, accusing the U.S. of trying to introduce last-minute demands that would limit Canada’s ability to make trade deals with other countries and protect its culture and sovereignty.

The U.S. introduced a new round of 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian exports on Saturday, targeting goods worth $28 billion. Canada announced retaliatory measures Tuesday that will go into effect Sept. 8.

content_blocks.text: Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is home to the country’s auto industry, said Monday that he backs Carney. He also took aim at Trump after the president posted about him on social media.

“I don’t respond to a dictator like President Trump, a bully like President Trump. I’m not going to take any advice off a guy that’s the king of bankruptcies,” Ford said during a news conference , which also heard him say Trump could “kiss my ass.”
“Let’s be clear, I don’t like the guy — simple.”
Ford told Cnn’s Wolf Blitzer Tuesday morning “things got a little personal” with Trump on Monday.
He said Trump’s Lake Ontario post was “a lot of rhetoric,” and it’s time to tone it down.
“I want to make a good deal for the American people, a good deal for the Canadians,” he said.

“We’re the two greatest countries in the world. We’re each other’s No. 1 customer and it’s time to get back to the table and let’s negotiate a fair deal because it’s hurting the U.S., it’s hurting Canada and we just want to make sure that we have a fair deal.”
Carney said Monday that Canada will go back to the negotiating table on a trade deal once the United States changes its attitude and stops treating Canada as a subsidiary.

stories.title: London library hunting for 125 missing high school yearbooks
stories.summary: The library is asking Londoners to donate yearbooks to help fill gaps in a collection dating back more than a century.
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
stories.content:
The library is asking Londoners to donate yearbooks to help fill gaps in a collection dating back more than a century.

If you have an old high school yearbook lying around, chances are the London Public Library might want it.

Exclusive articles from Ryan Pyette, Dale Carruthers, Jane Sims, Norman De Bono and others. Plus, the Noon News Roundup newsletter on weekdays and the LFP Weekender newsletter on weekends.

A new campaign from the library is asking Londoners to donate their high school yearbooks for its collection at the Ivey Family London Room, the London-specific archive at Central Library, 251 Dundas St.

David Caloren, the library’s coordinator of central adult services and supervisor of the London Room, says the campaign is a way to fill gaps in the collection.

“Yearbooks are not something you can just buy from a vendor, you have to be connected to the school in some way to get them,” he said. “We’ve relied on people giving them to US because we can’t really seek them out that way.”

Caloren says the library has been building its yearbook collection for decades, starting in the 1960s, and has volumes from 34 different high schools in London and the surrounding area – some of which have since closed.

He estimates there are more than 750 unique yearbooks stored at the London Public Library, all donated by Londoners over the years.

“We’ve never had a program of actively collecting them, they come to US sort of haphazardly,” Caloren said.

Caloren says yearbooks are especially valuable to researchers and Londoners because of their hyperlocal subject matter, often showing what was happening in a community and trends in fashion, music and clubs.

“They tell a lot about what was important for that particular community at that particular time,” he said.

They are also a good source for finding old photos of famous Londoners from when they were younger, he joked.

Caloren says the oldest official yearbook in the collection is from London Central Secondary School in 1922.

But the library also has documents dating back to 1903 that he describes as “yearbook-adjacent” – small, student-produced booklets that were never formally issued as yearbooks.

The library is currently looking for around 125 yearbooks to fill gaps in the collection, he says, but most of what it needs is fairly recent.

“I’m really hoping those Gen Z kids have a look. We’re missing a lot of the 2010 yearbooks and that would be a great score for US if we could fill in our gaps for this century,” Caloren said.

Some of the oldest material the library needs is from De La Salle High School, which closed in the 1950s. The collection has only one yearbook from the school.

Londoners looking to donate their high school yearbooks can contact the London Room by email at research.request@lpl.CA or by phone at 519-661-5100 ext. 2410.

stories.title: Dealer sentenced in London mother's fentanyl-tainted cocaine death
stories.summary: A judge said the dealer did not know the cocaine contained fentanyl, but his role still carried “devastating consequences.”
stories.author: Jane Sims
stories.content:
A judge said the dealer did not know the cocaine contained fentanyl, but his role still carried “devastating consequences.”

It was cocaine that everyone thought was clean – the street-drug dealer, his customer and his partner who died after ingesting it.

Exclusive articles from Ryan Pyette, Dale Carruthers, Jane Sims, Norman De Bono and others. Plus, the Noon News Roundup newsletter on weekdays and the LFP Weekender newsletter on weekends.

But the drugs that killed London mother Christina Bestward were part of what a judge described as “a troubling and increasingly common reality of the illicit drug trade: the contamination of street-level drugs with fentanyl.”

On Monday, Jordan Colley, 35, the drug dealer, was sentenced to a total of 42 months in prison for manslaughter in the death of Bestward, 41, and two years to be served concurrently for criminal negligence causing bodily harm to her partner, Daniel Gale, 39, ON May 12, 2023. Factoring in time already served, he has 35.5 months, or just under three years, left on his sentence.

“While fentanyl has attracted much of the recent public attention, cocaine remains a dangerous drug,” Superior Court Justice Marc Garson said. “The illicit drug trade operates in an environment where substances are frequently mixed, diluted, cut or contaminated. Users have little ability to know with confidence what they are consuming.”

“The facts of this case provide a stark illustration of that reality.”

Colley was convicted after a trial earlier this year in which Garson learned Colley didn’t know the cocaine he sold to Gale was contaminated with the highly potent opioid when he dropped it off at their Wyatt Street home.

Bestward and Gale had sent their young child to a relative’s home the night before so they could celebrate Bestward’s certification as a personal support worker. Gale was a cocaine addict, while Bestward was not a habitual drug user.

Gale had contacted Colley just after midnight to buy drugs and again early in the morning when the supply ran out. Colley delivered more drugs and Gale cooked them into crack. Both he and Bestward took a couple of tokes, and his last memory was walking into the living room before waking up in hospital.

The couple was found by their child after school. Gale was taken to hospital, but Bestward could not be revived.

Dealer convicted of manslaughter in overdose death; a first in London

Fentanyl, cocaine or both? Trial examines cause of London mom’s death

While other drug dealers have been convicted of manslaughter throughout the province for supplying deadly drugs to clients, Colley was the first to be convicted of the serious charge stemming from a London police investigation.

As Garson pointed out in his decision, the opioid crisis has had a stranglehold on communities across the country, but its grip has been even tighter on London.

Garson referred to statistics filed by the Crown that formed a community impact statement presented in other fentanyl-related cases and that “paints a deep and troubling picture.”

“Fentanyl-related overdoses, illnesses, hospitalizations and deaths have increased dramatically over the last decade,” Garson said. “Young adults between the ages of 25 and 44 have borne a disproportionate share of that harm.”

“Behind every death is grief. Parents bury children. Children lose parents. Friends, co-workers and entire communities are left to bear the consequences.”

Local death rates have exceeded provincial averages. In the first quarter of 2020, there were an estimated 100 accidental deaths involving fentanyl. A year later, the number doubled. London is now approaching 300 deaths due to fentanyl annually.

“London has borne a disproportionate share of this crisis,” Garson said, noting that at one point London police were recording 2.7 fentanyl-related deaths every 2.7 days and police time spent responding to fentanyl calls rose 400 per cent.

Pressure has also been put on emergency departments, hospitals, paramedics and community agencies.

“Scarce public resources continue to absorb the burden of a preventable crisis that shows little signs of abating,” Garson said.

Contamination of the street drug supply is a constant threat. Fentanyl is 80 to 100 times more powerful than morphine and it takes only a few milligrams to be lethal.

“When fentanyl contaminates another illicit substance, users often consume it without knowing what they have purchased or ingested. What appears to be a routine drug transaction can quickly turn fatal,” Garson said.

The Crown had argued for a six-year prison sentence, while the defence suggested a two-year-less-a-day conditional sentence with three years of probation.

Colley, Garson noted, had a positive pre-sentence report. He has matured from an unstable childhood. While he has a criminal record, including convictions for drug trafficking, he has maintained steady employment and “made meaningful efforts to improve himself.”

He was described as “generous, kind-hearted, caring and someone who would not intentionally harm others.” He has wide support from family, friends and his employer, all of whom were in the courtroom to support him.

And he has deep remorse for what happened to Bestward and Gale.

Garson commended Colley for his turnaround, but said his thoughts were with the victims and their loved ones. “They have suffered a profound, tragic and entirely unnecessary loss.”

While no victim impact statements were filed, Garson said he knows “those consequences will endure long after these proceedings have concluded.”

The case was a reminder “that those who choose to traffic in illicit drugs participate in a dangerous enterprise with potentially catastrophic consequences.”

“Mr. Colley did not know the cocaine he trafficked contained fentanyl. It reduced, but did not erase his culpability,” Garson said.

“His decision and choice to participate in the illicit drug trade had devastating consequences and the sentence I have imposed reflects both realities.”

stories.title: Ford government celebrates construction work on northern Ontario mining roads
stories.summary: On Monday, the Ontario government and Aroland First Nation announced that ground had broken on work to upgrade the Anaconda and Painter Lake roads, part of a broader network.
stories.author: Isaac Callan, Colin D'Mello
stories.content:
If you get Global News from Instagram or Facebook - that will be changing. Find out how you can still connect with US .

Construction work is officially underway on roads in a remote, mineral-rich area of northern Ontario as part of the Ford government’s push to open up the Ring of Fire for mining.

On Monday, the Ontario government and Aroland First Nation announced that ground had broken on work to upgrade the Anaconda and Painter Lake roads, part of a broader network in the region.

“By building the roads to the Ring of Fire , we are unlocking $22 billion in economic potential and 70,000 good-paying jobs, while working with partners like Aroland First Nation to improve access to services for community members,” Premier Doug Ford said in a statement.

“I want to thank Chief Sonny Gagnon and the members of Aroland First Nation for their partnership as we stand up to protect Ontario communities and workers.”

Since it was first elected in 2018, the Ford government has sought to create an all-season road to the Ring of Fire, which is home to remote First Nations as well as a range of critical minerals and potential mining opportunities.

The Ring of Fire is an area coveted by major mining companies for its range of critical minerals, which are key to various modern technologies like phones and batteries.

The Ford government put extra emphasis on building an all-season road to the area to make large-scale mining possible in the 2025 snap election.

The premier pitched it as a solution to make Ontario more economically self-sufficient and to give it resources that the United States May want to partner on.

Since winning the 2025 election, the government has accelerated work on the project, which has undergone expedited environmental assessments.

The construction work with Aroland First Nation is five years ahead of schedule, the government said Monday.

“Our government is making historic investments in our provincial highway network to unlock access to the Ring of Fire while supporting economic opportunities for First Nations in northern Ontario,” said Prabmeet Sarkaria, Minister of Transportation.

stories.title: 1 in 3 Ontario children are living in food-insecure homes: Breakfast Club of Canada
stories.summary: New data from Breakfast Club of Canada is showing students across the country are coming to class with an empty stomach, reflecting a larger issue of food insecurity in households.
stories.author: Megan King
stories.content:
As children prepare to head back to school, a nutritious meal will be an important way to start off their day.

New data from Breakfast Club of Canada is highlighting the growing need for programs to make sure it’s possible for all kids to receive those meals.

“Kids show up to school every day and, very often, don’t have the nutrition that they need to get through that day in a positive way or be their best selves at school,” said Ryan Baker, Breakfast Club of Canada programs lead.

“What we want to make sure is that every student has that ability and has that chance to be their best self.”

In Toronto alone, Breakfast Club of Canada supports 863 breakfast programs reaching more than 250,000 children.

According to the non-profit organization, one in three Ontario children lives in a household affected by food insecurity — while nearly 2.4 million children across Canada face that reality.

“We know that universal programs, they improve health by promoting food and nutrition security, they encourage long-term healthy eating habits and they support student’s mental and physical health,” said Tara Galloro with the City of Toronto.

Galloro is a policy development officer with the city’s poverty reduction office.

This fall, Toronto’s Student Nutrition Program will expand to an additional 78 public schools in the city, marking the final phase of its universal morning meal program.

However, University of Toronto professor emerita Valerie Tarasuk thinks food is only part of the story.

“By the time the household is struggling to put food on the table, they are struggling with a whole lot of things: utility payments, telecommunications, rent, transportation, you name it. Food is just one part of the budget,” said Tarasuk.

She sees children coming to school without breakfast as a signal that there’s a bigger problem to tackle — household economic issues that require government assistance.

“We just have to go back to the drawing board a little bit and say, ‘How come we have this problem?’ What better could we be doing with these benefit programs to make sure they’re reaching people who need them and they’re providing adequate support,” Tarasuk added.

The Canada Child Benefit and Ontario Child Benefit are currently in place to help low-income families provide for children under 18. Tarasuk wants to see those improved upon.

stories.title: Western University’s free legal clinic moving closer to London courthouse
stories.summary: The clinic is expected to relocate to Fanshawe’s downtown campus in late December.
stories.author: Allison Young
stories.content:
The clinic is expected to relocate to Fanshawe’s downtown campus in late December.

Western University ’s legal clinic is moving downtown, with officials saying the new location will help bring free legal assistance to more low-income and marginalized people in London and Middlesex County.

Exclusive articles from Ryan Pyette, Dale Carruthers, Jane Sims, Norman De Bono and others. Plus, the Noon News Roundup newsletter on weekdays and the LFP Weekender newsletter on weekends.

Community Legal Services, a clinic operated by Western’s Faculty of Law, is expected to move into its new location on the fifth floor of Fanshawe College’s Howard W. Rundle Building on Dundas Street in late December.

The clinic will continue operating from the Josephine Spencer Niblett Law Building on Western’s campus while renovations are completed at the downtown location.

“This move marks a major milestone in strengthening community-based legal services to ensure people in London and region can access critical support that May otherwise be out of reach,” Western president Alan Shepard said.

The move will bring Community Legal Services closer to the London courthouse, which Western officials say will make legal assistance more accessible to potential clients.

“We’re pleased to have Western’s Community Legal Services clinic join US, strengthening the goals we’ve always had for our downtown campus – creating exceptional learning opportunities for students while contributing to the continued growth and vibrancy of the city’s core,” Fanshawe president Peter Devlin said.

Devlin and Shepard signed the lease for the new space Monday.

Community Legal Services gives law students hands-on experience assisting with cases involving criminal law, small claims of up to $50,000, tenant and housing disputes, provincial offences and family law.

Over the 2025-26 academic year, Western students took on more than 600 cases and consultations.

“I’ve seen how even a simple housing issue can snowball and affect people for the rest of their lives,” he said. “Our work helps clients and, in some cases, their children recover from the lasting effects of those experiences. With support from CLS, they can move on with their lives.”

stories.title: Trump’s 50% auto tariff threat rattles Southwestern Ontario manufacturers
stories.summary: Industry experts warn the threatened tariffs could devastate Canada’s auto sector while also disrupting U.S. production.
stories.author: Jonathan Juha
stories.content:
Industry experts warn the threatened tariffs could devastate Canada’s auto sector while also disrupting U.S. production.

Southwestern Ontario manufacturers reacted with surprise and disbelief Monday to U.S. President Donald Trump’s threat to slap 50-per-cent tariffs on Canadian vehicles and auto parts, with one calling it “a nuclear option” that could decimate the region’s auto parts industry while also inflicting pain south of the border.

Exclusive articles from Ryan Pyette, Dale Carruthers, Jane Sims, Norman De Bono and others. Plus, the Noon News Roundup newsletter on weekdays and the LFP Weekender newsletter on weekends.

Trump said he planned to impose the new tariffs starting Jan. 1, a move that comes after trade negotiations between the U.S. and Canada broke down Friday, resulting in 50-per-cent levies now being applied on about $28-billion worth of Canadian goods, ON top of sector-specific tariffs already applied to autos, steel and aluminum.

“On January First, 2027, Tariffs on all Cars, Trucks, both large and small, Automotive Parts, and Steel, will be increased to 50%,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “Build in the U.S. and there are Zero Tariffs. Canada will be treated like a State no longer!

There was an error, please provide a valid email address.

Interested in more newsletters? Browse here.

“On Trade, and in other ways, also, they are among the worst Nations in the World to deal with.”

For his part, Prime Minister Mark Carney has said Canada will retaliate with dollar-for-dollar tariffs of its own beginning Sept. 8.

Industry watchers said Monday the potential new tariffs would be devastating for Ontario’s auto belt, a key economic driver for the province that extends from Guelph, Cambridge and Woodstock in the east to Windsor in the west and includes four auto plants and dozens of parts makers along the Highway 401 corridor.

“That’s like a nuclear bomb kind of effect that would be bad for everyone,” said Ben Whitney, owner of Armo Tool Ltd. in London, a manufacturer of machinery used to make parts for the automotive, defence and food and beverage sectors, among others.

“There is no auto parts industry in Canada with that, but this would be extremely difficult for the entire automotive industry. This is a 50 per cent tariff in a sector that’s making six or seven (per cent) in profit margins, so something’s going to give.”

Flavio Volpe, president of Canada’s Automotive Parts Manufacturers’ Association, echoed that assessment, saying U.S. automakers would also suffer from such a move.

Can defence spending save Ontario's auto-parts sector?

London firms among manufacturers eyeing U.S. investment as tariffs bite

“The ‘importer of record’ pays the tariffs. A threatened U.S. tariff on Canadian auto parts will be paid by U.S. auto assembly,” he wrote on X, formerly Twitter.

“Without those specific parts, auto assembly throughout the U.S. would halt.”

Dave Johnson, general manager at London-based Ursa Manufacturing ULC, said the levies are so high it would take time to determine exactly how they would affect his company, which makes stampings and light assemblies for companies including General Motors Co. and Toyota Boshoku Corp.

“But if that is the case, quite potentially, all automotive in North America would stop moving,” he said.

“Whether it will occur or not is one thing, but it has the potential to bring the entire automotive industry to a halt . . . so let’s hope this is more bluster and bluff because it seems like a total shot in the dark that (Trump) is taking. The automotive companies, I would imagine, will have some sort of response to that.”

Currently, the Canadian auto sector faces a 25 per cent tariff on vehicles exported to the U.S., but that amount can be reduced based on the percentage of U.S. content in a vehicle.

It wasn’t immediately clear Monday whether the U.S. government would continue to apply that exemption to parts produced south of the border.

But even if it did, it would still represent an effective tariff rate of 25 per cent for automakers in Canada, said Greig Mordue, an associate professor at McMaster University’s Booth School of Engineering Practice and Technology.

Mordue, who questioned whether Trump “understands what he’s done,” given how intertwined the auto sector is, didn’t mince words when describing the potential impact of tariffs at that level on Canada’s industry.

“Frankly, an effective rate of 25 percent expedites the demise of the Canadian automotive manufacturing industry,” he said.

Mordue noted the move would put Japanese automakers Honda Motor Co., Ltd. and Toyota Motor Corporation, which so far have absorbed the cost of tariffs, in a difficult position. Unlike Ford Motor Co., General Motors Co. and Stellantis NV, Mordue said neither Honda nor Toyota has idle capacity to shift some production to the U.S.

And while the Japanese companies May have been willing to continue with a wait-and-see approach at current tariff levels, pending the results of the November midterm elections or a new administration in 2029, the potential new tariff levels change the equation, with Mordue pegging the financial hit for both manufacturers at about $10 billion.

“They would look at that and say, ‘We can’t put any new product or commit to new models at that level,’” he said.

“They like building cars in Canada. They’ve made a commitment to Canada, and they think that commitment is a long-term one to Canada . . . but they can’t look at their global operations and say Canada is going to absorb half of their profitability globally.”

stories.title: ‘Bring it on buddy’: Everything Ontario’s Doug Ford said about President Donald Trump
stories.summary: Over the course of 45 minutes, Doug Ford said Donald Trump could 'kiss my ass,' calling him a 'dictator,' a 'loser' and the 'king of bankruptcies.'
stories.author: Isaac Callan
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford fired a series of insults and threats at United States President Donald Trump on Monday afternoon in a growing war of words between the two leaders.

Moments before the Ontario premier’s press conference began, Trump posted on his Truth Social platform, accusing him of “bluster” in trade talks and calling him a “flunky.”

“Lots of ‘bluster’ from Doug Ford, who is the Premier of the Canadian Province of Ontario, but who is better known as the less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother of the late, great, Rob Ford,” Trump wrote around 2 p.m. on Monday.

The premier responded throughout his news conference with insults, threats and pledges to try and make sure the Republicans lose crucial midterm elections this fall.

Here is everything Doug Ford said about Donald Trump answering questions from reporters on Monday afternoon:

“I have a lot of real estate on my ass, so (Trump) has a lot of room to kiss my ass. I just do. I’m a big dude. What can I say?

I don’t respond to a dictator like President Trump, a bully like President Trump. As I said before, he’s the type of guy in school that would take your lunch money one day, take your toque off your head the next day, and then steal your running shoes. But I’m not going to take any advice off a guy that’s the king of bankruptcies. He’s actually tariffing his own people, taxing his own people.

“I’m not going to take lessons off President Trump, he’s the last guy that I would take any lessons off. It’s about Team Canada. We’ll see how this goes but he wants to put pain on Canadians, we’ll leverage every bit of pain we possibly can on Americans. I’ve always said I love the American people. I still stand by that statement because there’s a lot of people in the U.S. that are calling me saying, ‘Way to go, keep going.’

You know your own people, President Trump, don’t even like you. And they’re going to speak loud and clear when it comes to the midterms. And if I was allowed to, I’d be down there door-knocking.

“I’ve been in this game a lot longer than he has. I got a skin on me like an alligator. And you think an insult from him hurts me? Well, bring it on, buddy. I’m ready. Bring it on. I’ve dealt with guys like you my whole life, and guess what? You all become losers because you’re a loser.

“We’ll use every tool in our toolbox, then we’ll see if President Trump says, ‘Do I need Canada?’ Watch how he does cartwheels and he shouts and screams when we put the (export electricity) surcharge on. As a matter of fact, I can’t wait — I cannot wait. Let’s be clear: I don’t like the guy. Simple.

“I’m not going to take the bait. This guy’s a loser, he’s going to be a loser, simple as that. We’re going to fight with everything we have. And, you know something? I have more courage, more brains in my baby toe than he has in his whole body.”

stories.title: Niagara police renew call for help solving case of 8 horses stabbed last year
stories.summary: Six of the horses received treatment on-site, one was taken for emergency care at a veterinary hospital for emergency care and one was found dead on the scene.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Police in the Niagara Region are renewing their calls for the public’s help as they continue to investigate an animal cruelty incident involving multiple horses one year ago.

It was July 31, 2025, when Niagara Regional Police Service launched an investigation after farm staff in Welland, Ont., discovered eight of the animals had suffered injuries “consistent with cuts or stab wounds” during a routine morning check. It’s believed the incident took place some time between July 30 and July 31.

The incident occurred at a horse boarding farm located near Buchner Road and Highway 140.

Six of the horses received treatment on-site, but one was taken to an out-of-town veterinary hospital for emergency care. One horse was also found dead on the scene.

Niagara police called the incident a “disturbing act of animal cruelty.”

A year later, police issued a renewed request on Monday for the public’s help in providing information that could help push the investigation forward.

Anyone with information is urged to call police at 905-688-4111, option three, then dial extension 1009487.

Anonymous tips can also be made to Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477 or online.

— with files from Global News’ Gabby Rodrigues

stories.title: OPP warn of scammers pretending to be police, spoofing phone numbers
stories.summary: Scammers are repeatedly calling Ontario residents claiming to be OPP officers, with some using technology to spoof the phone numbers of OPP detachments.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) are issuing a warning to the public amid an ongoing phone scam in which people are pretending to be members of the police force and even spoofing their phone numbers.

Scammers have been calling people in the province repeatedly and identifying themselves as police officers.

The scammers May ask about ongoing investigations, request personal information, or in some cases try to obtain sensitive details under the guise of it helping with a police matter. By making repeated calls, police say scammers are trying to add pressure onto individuals to respond.

It’s not just repeated calls, either.

OPP say fraudsters are using spoofing technology to make it appear as though the calls are coming from a legitimate police number, specifically that of the Sudbury OPP. That phone number is 705-564-6900.

By doing so, police say it May make the call seem even more credible and increase the likelihood members of the public will answer and speak with the scammers.

People are reminded that police will never request sensitive personal or financial information over the phone.

“These calls are fraudulent and are an attempt to deceive individuals into providing information that could be used for criminal purposes,” OPP said in a release.

The public is asked to remain vigilant as scam calls continue to grow in frequency and reminded to take several precautions.

Don’t provide personal or financial information to unsolicited callers.

Be cautious of repeated calls and do not feel pressured to respond.

Do not rely solely on caller ID, as phone numbers are being spoofed.

Verify the identity of the caller by contacting your local police detachment directly using publicly listed phone numbers.

Be cautious of any caller creating a sense of urgency or pressure.

If you receive a suspicious call claiming to be from police, hang up and report the incident to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre at 1-888-495-8501. You can also contact them online.

Anyone with information about these incidents is also asked to contact Nipissing West OPP at 1-888-310-1122.

paragraphs: London, ON (August 21, 2026) – A London man is facing a number of charges after police located an unconscious driver in the east end of the city last night.

On Thursday, August 20, 2026, at approximately 8 p.m., an off-duty London police officer observed a vehicle stopped on Florence Street near Kellogg Lane. As the officer approached to check on the driver, the vehicle began moving and struck a nearby fence. As he approached the vehicle, a man was found unconscious behind the wheel. The officer called 9-1-1 and police and paramedic services attended.
The suspect male was arrested without incident.
A search resulted in the seizure of the following items:
- 254 grams of suspected cocaine, value: $25,400
- Quantity of Canadian currency
As a result of the investigation, James Beretta, 29, of London, has been charged with the following offences:
- Occupy motor vehicle with firearm;
- Careless storage of a firearm, weapon, prohibited device;
- Possess restricted or prohibited firearm knowingly not holding a licence and registration certificate;
- Possession of a prohibited or restricted weapon or prohibited device;
- Impaired operation of a conveyance;
- Possess loaded or unloaded regulated firearm;
- Possession of a Schedule I substance for the purpose of trafficking.
The accused is scheduled to appear in London court today in relation to the charges.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips (8477). Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers.
For media inquiries, contact:
Non-Emergency: 519-661-5670
